Elena — great to talk earlier. Following up with the written proposal you requested. High level: Redwood can agree to a narrowly scoped SLA exemption for failures caused by content-moderation filter halts or tool-call sanitization that cause structured-output or tool execution failures, provided we put the following mitigations and commitments in place. I’ve attached a draft exemption clause (exemption-draft-cloudcorp-v1.docx) and the filter incident log we reviewed.

Proposed exemption summary (plain language):
- Scope: exemption applies only to production incidents where (a) Redwood’s content moderation pipeline returns a blocking classification that prevents downstream tool-calls or structured-output serialization, and (b) the only available remediation is content edit or human review (i.e., not a transient compute/infra outage).
- Duration: exemption may be invoked for individual incidents; Redwood will not claim a blanket long-term removal of SLO coverage.
- Limits: total number of exempted incidents per 12-month term capped at 6 for CloudCorp, beyond which standard SLA credits will apply.

Mitigations we will commit to if exemption accepted:
1) Instrumentation: Real-time filter telemetry exported to a shared CloudCorp dashboard (Drive link included). Alerts on any filter-induced tool-call failures within 2 minutes.
2) Automated retries + deterministic fallbacks: For tool-calls that fail due to escaping/sanitization, Redwood will attempt up to 2 automated, low-latency sanitization retries with preserved semantics before returning a blocking error.
3) Graceful degradation: When structured-output generation is blocked, Redwood will attempt a fallback generation mode (constrained template output) which preserves essential fields; if fallback produces incomplete output, the response will include a standardized error payload so CloudCorp can choose client-side UI behaviour.
4) Human-in-the-loop escalation for repeat offenders: If a given CloudCorp customer prompt (or template) triggers the same blocking classification > 3 times in 24 hours, Redwood will automatically open an incident with CloudCorp ops and provide suggested prompt adjustments and a one-off manual review within 8 business hours.
5) Postmortems & credits: Any incident that falls under the exemption will have a P1 postmortem within 72 hours and a remediation plan. If we exceed the per-year exemption cap, or if the mitigation controls fail to operate as defined, standard SLA credits will apply retroactively.

Proposed measurable SLOs while exemption is active:
- Detection: 99% of filter-induced tool failures are detected and alerted within 2 minutes.
- Retry success: Automated sanitization retries convert at least 40% of eligible failures into successful tool-calls during peak.
- Fallback availability: Constrained-output fallback returns a valid payload (possibly partial) for 95% of blocked structured-output attempts.
- Postmortem cadence: 100% of exempt incidents have a postmortem produced within 72 hours.

Proposed credit model if mitigation targets are missed:
- For missed Detection SLOs: 5% service credit per missed incident up to a maximum of 25% for the billing month.
- For Retry success or Fallback availability misses: fixed $2,500 per missed incident beyond the exemption cap. (Open to negotiating in contract.)

Next steps: we’d like to get feedback on the scope/limits and whether Procurement needs different credit formulas. Marcus and Karthik (cc’d) can own the technical acceptance criteria and instrumentation details. Lauren will field legal/contract redlines.

Vanessa / team —

Quick tech context to support the proposal: the incidents in the attached CSV are dominated by two failure patterns: (A) token-level sanitization mismatch that causes JSON-structured output to break at serialization time, and (B) tool-call payloads flagged for PII patterns that require deterministic redaction. For (A) our retry + constrained-template fallback works well; for (B) the human-in-the-loop path is often required because automated redaction risks removing required fields.

Operational notes:
- We can export the filter telemetry to CloudCorp with ~30s ingestion latency and a per-alert webhook. We’ll need CloudCorp to authorize a read-only API key.
- The automated sanitization path increases per-request CPU by ~6–12% (depends on payload size). If CloudCorp wants these retries by default, we should discuss cost-sharing or toggles per route.
- For the fallback mode, we’ll publish a deterministic template schema mapping that CloudCorp can validate against.

I’ll draft a short appendix (technical acceptance criteria) that maps each SLO to a metric and the alerting thresholds.

—Marcus
